record.title: Background processes started by an approval-free exec outlive the exec's timeout, so one exec can leave the sandbox pinned at its pids limit
record.description: An agent token sends an approval-free exec whose command is many backgrounded allowlisted programs (tail -f /dev/null & x1100 + tail -f /dev/null). policy.simple_programs splits on & so every segment is tail and read-only-exec returns allow. sandbox.exec runs timeout -k 5 <exec_timeout> bash -c 'umask 002\n' + command; GNU timeout signals the process group only when its deadline fires, so when bash exits first (here by fork failure once pids.max is reached) timeout returns bash's status and never kills the group, leaving the backgrounded children running and the container pinned at pids.max. The candidate was raised as needs_validation on whether the pinned state reaches beyond the agent's own sandbox and which human recovery actions still work.
record.claimed_root_cause: exec's only bound on agent-started work is GNU timeout around bash (sandbox.py:531), which does not reap background children when bash exits before the deadline; nothing else (process-group kill after the exec, per-exec pids cap, or cleanup) bounds processes an allowlisted exec leaves behind, so they persist and can hold the container at pids.max.

trace.description: Agent token sends exec with a command made of many backgrounded allowlisted programs. Verified: call_tool at api.py:205-211.
tail is allowlisted (default_policy.yaml:24-25); policy.simple_programs splits on & so every segment is tail and policy.decide returns allow without approval. Verified in source and by h-policy.
timeout -k 5 <t> bash -c 'umask 002\n'+command; no process-group cleanup after exec_inspect. Verified: background children are not reaped when bash exits before the deadline.

evidence.description: exec_create argv is timeout -k 5 str(t) bash -c 'umask 002\n' + command; exec_inspect reads ExitCode with no process-group cleanup. Confirmed verbatim at sandbox.py:531-537.
desktop_pids default 1024 (AGENTBOX_DESKTOP_PIDS); config.py:40 pids_limit default 256 for other templates. Confirmed.

v16 local sbx5 repro of the mechanism: timeout -k 5 30 bash -c '(loop)& exit 0' returned exit 0 and the backgrounded child SURVIVED unreaped after timeout returned (deadline never fired, so no group kill). Confirms the sink's claimed behavior.

Parent-live recovery probe (re-read and judged sound): while the sandbox is pinned at pids.max, a concurrent 'other sandbox exec' succeeds, human snapshot/pause/resume succeed, and human restore instantly returns pids to baseline (254/256->2/256; 1022/1024->8/1024) after which the agent execs normally; delete succeeds. Only in-container execs on the SAME sandbox degrade (read_file fails 'Cannot fork' in ~0.1s).

record.reason: Mechanism confirmed, material/shared impact refuted during validation. The trace and evidence are source-accurate: sandbox.py:531 wraps the command in timeout -k 5 <t> bash -c; GNU timeout signals the group only at its deadline; read-only-exec (default_policy.yaml:24-25) allowlists tail and policy.simple_programs splits on & so 'tail -f /dev/null & ...' runs approval-free (confirmed in policy.py and by h-policy). I reproduced the core mechanism locally in sbx5 (agents/v16/artifacts/v16_mechanism.out): when bash exits before the deadline, timeout returns bash's status and the backgrounded child survives unreaped, so nothing bounds processes an allowlisted exec leaves behind. The candidate was needs_validation solely on its blocker: whether the pinned state reaches beyond the agent's own sandbox and which human recovery actions work. Parent-live l11_pinned_recovery (owner-observed local evidence I re-read and judged sound; it creates a pinned sandbox plus a second 'other' sandbox on both cli and desktop templates and runs every recovery action) resolves that blocker against the vulnerability: a concurrent other-sandbox exec succeeds (no cross-sandbox or control-plane blast radius), human snapshot/pause/resume all succeed, and human restore instantly returns pids to baseline, after which the agent execs normally; human delete also succeeds. The only degradation is in-container tool execs on the same sandbox (read_file fails 'Cannot fork' in ~0.1s, immediately releasing its tool_pool thread, so no shared resource is retained). This is self-limiting availability of the requester's own sandbox with complete operator recovery and no shared blast radius, which this domain's discipline classifies as hardening, not a service vulnerability ('Self-limiting work in the requester's own process is not a service vulnerability'; 'do not validate with availability impact'). The GUI-burst fail-open that this same pids pressure can cause is a distinct shared-safety-function claim owned by v09 (service.py:_open_gui_burst), which the prompt directs me not to credit to this candidate. No source or local observation supports a shared, cross-principal, or persistent-beyond-operator-control impact, so the candidate is refuted.
